PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 44 — Lesson 68: Musculoskeletal Assessment & Diagnostics

FNP-level goal: Evaluate back pain, acute joint complaints, extremity injury, and generalized musculoskeletal symptoms using mechanism, function, focused examination, appropriate imaging, and diagnostic safety. Identify fracture, septic arthritis, spinal cord/cauda equina compromise, infection, malignancy, neurovascular injury, DVT/vascular mimics, and other presentations that cannot safely remain in routine outpatient care.

Learning Objectives

  • Create a problem representation for musculoskeletal pain using onset, trauma, location, inflammatory features, function, and systemic risk.
  • Perform and document a focused spine, joint, and extremity examination, including neurovascular status when relevant.
  • Recognize red flags in low-back pain, acute monoarthritis, injury, and inability to bear weight.
  • Differentiate mechanical, inflammatory, infectious, crystal, traumatic, neurologic, vascular, and referred pain patterns.
  • Choose imaging and laboratory studies to answer a defined clinical question.
  • Build safe disposition, referral, and follow-up plans.

Part 1 — Musculoskeletal Complaints Start With Function and Safety

Before naming a diagnosis, assess stability and function. Can the patient bear weight, transfer, use the affected limb, protect the airway after trauma, and safely leave clinic? Check vital signs, appearance, severe pain, mechanism, anticoagulants, age/frailty, osteoporosis risk, immune compromise, diabetes, cancer history, fever, and ability to obtain help. An apparently “orthopedic” complaint can be infectious, vascular, neurologic, abdominal, cardiopulmonary, or medication-related.

Emergency evaluation is appropriate for major trauma, deformity with neurovascular concern, open fracture, suspected dislocation, cold/pale or pulseless limb, rapidly worsening pain/swelling, compartment-syndrome concern, inability to bear weight after significant injury, sepsis concern, acute spinal neurologic compromise, or pain with physiologic instability. Stabilize, immobilize when indicated, and use local emergency pathways rather than extending a routine outpatient examination.

Part 2 — Build the Problem Representation

Clarify onset and mechanism: sudden or gradual; traumatic, repetitive, spontaneous, or postinfectious; first episode or recurrent; focal or diffuse; unilateral or symmetric; constant, movement-related, nocturnal, or inflammatory. Ask about fever, malaise, rash, recent infection, travel/tick exposure where relevant, joint injection/prosthesis/surgery, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, cancer, steroid exposure, IV drug use, weight loss, neurologic symptoms, bowel/bladder changes, and medication/substance use.

Describe the functional consequence: ability to bear weight, grip, walk, sleep, dress, work, climb stairs, or perform activities of daily living. Pain severity alone does not establish seriousness; trajectory, context, systemic features, objective function, and examination determine the differential and disposition.

Part 3 — Focused Examination: Look, Feel, Move, Function

Inspect both sides for swelling, erythema, warmth, bruising, deformity, asymmetry, atrophy, rash, scars, wounds, and posture. Palpate systematically for focal bony tenderness, joint-line tenderness, warmth, effusion, crepitus, muscle spasm, and compartments that are tense or disproportionately painful. Assess active range of motion first when safe, then passive range of motion if appropriate. Compare strength, sensation, distal pulses, capillary refill, and function.

For acute injury, document the neurovascular examination before and after immobilization or any maneuver. Avoid forcing a painful joint through range of motion or attempting a reduction without the appropriate setting, training, analgesia, and imaging pathway. Negative plain radiographs do not always exclude clinically important fracture, tendon injury, infection, or occult injury when history and function remain concerning.

Part 4 — Acute Monoarthritis: Infection Until Appropriately Excluded

An acutely painful, swollen, warm joint has a broad differential: septic arthritis, crystal arthritis, hemarthrosis, trauma, inflammatory arthritis, reactive arthritis, and periarticular disease. Fever may be absent, especially in older adults, immunocompromised patients, and patients taking antipyretics. Risk rises with prosthetic joints, recent procedure, bacteremia, skin infection, diabetes, immune compromise, injection drug use, inflammatory arthritis, and other comorbidities.

Septic arthritis is a joint-threatening emergency. Do not assume that known gout, osteoarthritis, a prior crystal flare, or a normal-appearing vital sign excludes infection. A hot swollen joint with marked pain, limited motion, systemic symptoms, or high-risk context needs urgent evaluation; synovial-fluid assessment and treatment decisions belong in the appropriate urgent/emergency pathway. Do not start an empiric outpatient steroid course merely because the joint “looks like gout” when infection remains plausible.

Part 5 — Crystal, Inflammatory, and Mechanical Patterns

Crystal arthritis often presents with abrupt severe inflammatory joint pain, but its pattern can overlap with infection. Inflammatory arthritis may involve prolonged morning stiffness, swelling, multiple joints, extra-articular symptoms, and a different functional trajectory than mechanical osteoarthritis. Mechanical pain is often activity-related and may improve with rest, but no single descriptor proves the diagnosis.

Use pattern recognition to construct a differential—not to close it prematurely. Confirm whether pain is intra-articular, periarticular, bony, neuropathic, referred, or diffuse. Review prior aspiration results, imaging, renal/hepatic function, anticoagulants, immunosuppressants, and medications before considering treatment, while recognizing that diagnostic urgency can override a routine medication decision.

Part 6 — Low Back Pain: Screen for the Dangerous Exceptions

Most low-back pain is not an emergency, but the FNP evaluation must actively screen for serious pathology. Ask about major trauma; minor trauma in an older or osteoporotic person; known cancer; unexplained weight loss; fever; immune compromise; injection drug use; recent infection; prolonged steroid use; progressive motor weakness; gait change; urinary retention or overflow incontinence; fecal incontinence; loss of anal tone; saddle sensory loss; and severe unrelenting or night pain.

New urinary retention/overflow incontinence, saddle anesthesia, bowel dysfunction, or progressive/global lower-extremity weakness can signal cauda equina syndrome or other severe neurologic compromise. Fever, immune compromise, bacteremia risk, or severe persistent back pain may raise concern for spinal infection. These patterns require emergency assessment; do not send the patient home with routine exercises and an outpatient MRI order.

Part 7 — Radiculopathy, Myelopathy, and Referred Pain

Radicular symptoms follow a nerve-root distribution and may include radiating pain, numbness, paresthesia, weakness, or reflex changes. Myelopathy can create broader cord-level findings such as gait dysfunction, upper-motor-neuron signs, hand clumsiness, or bowel/bladder change. Compare sides, test functional strength, and document the neurologic pattern. A normal straight-leg raise or normal isolated strength test does not exclude a serious evolving process in the wrong clinical setting.

Back, hip, shoulder, and limb pain can be referred. Consider abdominal aortic disease, renal disease, pelvic disease, cardiopulmonary disease, malignancy, herpes zoster, peripheral arterial disease, DVT, and neurologic causes when symptoms, physiology, or risk factors do not fit a simple mechanical explanation.

Part 8 — Injury, Fracture, and Occult Fracture

Mechanism, focal bony tenderness, inability to bear weight, age/frailty, osteoporosis, anticoagulant use, and pain trajectory help assess fracture risk. Plain radiographs are often an appropriate initial study for acute traumatic bony injury, but an initially negative or indeterminate radiograph does not automatically end evaluation when clinical suspicion for hip or other occult fracture remains high. Advanced imaging and urgent orthopedic/emergency evaluation may be needed according to the injury, examination, and local pathway.

Distinguish soft-tissue pain from bony tenderness and assess adjacent joints. After a fall, do not assume the patient’s baseline ambulation or a prior arthritis diagnosis explains new inability to bear weight. In older adults especially, occult fracture, head injury, bleeding risk, and loss of safe mobility may matter as much as the isolated painful joint.

Part 9 — Neurovascular and Compartment Safety

For extremity trauma, ask about numbness, weakness, coolness, color change, escalating pain, pain with passive stretch, and tight swelling. Examine pulses, capillary refill, sensation, motor function, skin temperature, and compartments. A palpable pulse does not rule out all serious vascular injury; changes from baseline, progressive symptoms, and the mechanism matter.

Disproportionate escalating pain, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, paresthesia, pallor, paralysis, or pulselessness can indicate a limb-threatening process and requires immediate emergency care. Do not delay transfer to complete a full outpatient musculoskeletal workup when neurovascular compromise or compartment syndrome is a concern.

Part 10 — Labs, Imaging, and Aspiration: Ask a Question

Testing should answer a hypothesis. CBC, inflammatory markers, metabolic studies, creatine kinase, uric acid, blood cultures, and other labs can provide context but cannot alone exclude septic arthritis, spinal infection, or fracture. A serum uric acid level does not diagnose the cause of an acutely inflamed joint. When joint infection or crystal disease is a key question, synovial-fluid analysis may be necessary in the appropriate setting.

Choose imaging based on the suspected structure and urgency: radiographs for many acute bony injuries; ultrasound for selected effusion or soft-tissue questions; MRI for selected occult fracture, tendon/ligament, spinal, or marrow/soft-tissue questions; and CT when it answers a trauma or bony-anatomy question. Use current local radiology criteria and consultation pathways. Imaging supports clinical reasoning; it does not replace emergency disposition in an unstable or limb-threatening presentation.

Part 11 — Medication, Comorbidity, and Diagnostic Safety

Medication review changes both the differential and treatment safety. Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase bleeding/hemarthrosis risk; systemic or injected corticosteroids can affect infection and fracture risk; fluoroquinolones and statins can be relevant to selected tendon or muscle complaints; immunosuppressants and biologics change infection risk; diuretics can influence crystal risk; and sedatives or antihypertensives may contribute to falls. Do not tell a patient to stop a high-stakes medication without understanding why it was prescribed and arranging a safe plan.

Outpatient management requires stable physiology, reasonable exclusion or escalation of high-consequence alternatives, safe mobility, pain control compatible with the patient’s comorbidities, and reliable follow-up. Give specific precautions for fever, red/hot swelling, rapidly worsening pain, numbness/weakness, color/coolness change, bowel/bladder symptoms, inability to bear weight, new trauma, or failure to improve.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Back Pain With a Red Flag

A 58-year-old with low-back pain now reports new urinary retention, numbness in the perineal region, and worsening bilateral leg weakness.

FNP reasoning: this is not routine sciatica. The combination raises concern for cauda equina syndrome or another severe neurologic process. Assess stability and arrange immediate emergency evaluation; an outpatient analgesic trial and delayed imaging are unsafe.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: The Hot Knee

A 71-year-old with diabetes and a knee replacement has acute knee pain, warmth, swelling, and severe pain with motion. They report no fever.

FNP reasoning: absence of fever does not exclude septic arthritis or prosthetic-joint infection. The high-risk context and inflammatory joint demand urgent evaluation; do not anchor on osteoarthritis or gout.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: Fall With “Normal” Initial X-Ray

An 82-year-old on anticoagulation falls, has groin pain, and cannot safely bear weight. Initial radiographs are read as negative.

FNP reasoning: inability to bear weight and risk context keep occult hip fracture and other injury on the differential. Ensure safe disposition and escalate for further evaluation/imaging according to the clinical pathway rather than reassuring the patient solely because initial films are negative.

FNP Musculoskeletal-Assessment Framework

  1. Assess safety and function: trauma, vitals, ability to bear weight/use the limb, and neurovascular status.
  2. Define the pattern: onset, mechanism, location, inflammatory/systemic symptoms, and trajectory.
  3. Examine deliberately: look → feel → move → function; compare sides and document distal neurovascular findings.
  4. Screen for red flags: infection, fracture, cancer, spinal compromise, compartment syndrome, vascular injury, and unsafe mobility.
  5. Keep a broad differential: mechanical, inflammatory, crystal, infectious, traumatic, neurologic, vascular, and referred causes.
  6. Test with a question: labs, aspiration, radiographs, ultrasound, MRI, CT, or emergency referral based on the clinical question.
  7. Close the loop: specific return precautions, safe mobility plan, result ownership, and timely reassessment.

High-Yield Summary

Acute hot swollen joint: treat septic arthritis as a critical alternative until appropriately excluded.
Low-back pain: screen for cancer/infection/fracture risk and cauda equina/spinal neurologic red flags.
Cauda equina warning signs: new urinary retention/overflow incontinence, saddle sensory loss, bowel dysfunction, or progressive weakness require emergency evaluation.
Trauma: assess mechanism, focal bony tenderness, function, and neurovascular status; a negative initial radiograph does not always exclude occult injury.
Neurovascular concern: escalating disproportionate pain, color/coolness change, sensory/motor deficit, or tense swelling is limb-threatening until proven otherwise.
Testing: should answer a defined question; labs and imaging support but do not replace emergency disposition.
FNP standard: integrate function, pattern, examination, risk, diagnostics, safe mobility, referral, and explicit return precautions.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Musculoskeletal assessment, injury care, imaging, aspiration, treatment, referral, and emergency disposition must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
